The butterflies are reported to be the piece-de-resistance of England's most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year. The Daily Mail once even asked: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" due to his looks and his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often referred to in a disparaging way. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page upon page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and her lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. There has also been fierce criticism over the fact she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. It's all down to Rooney apparently, and nothing to do with her appearing to be quite a decent person, who did well at school and has cleverly managed to parlay some of her fame into various media and advertising projects. Anyone who has seen her television show -- Coleen's Real Women -- can see she is a decent, bubbly person, who is very good at putting people at ease. Much to the media's fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to OK magazine for a record $5 million. However they're not pocketing all the cash themselves, with an undisclosed sum from the fee to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire -- where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister Rosie is cared for. The queen's grandson, Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly, recently received $1m from Hello magazine to cover their wedding but they didn't receive an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous, but lower class, Rooney and McLoughlin. Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have also asked guests to donate money to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool. The wedding might be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests (they are covering the guests' costs), expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress, but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for critics. It's just not on that someone who wasn't born into privilege and didn't go to a posh school can enjoy their wealth. That would be ugly. If anything, the couple's relationship and success is a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, but she spent two years fending off Rooney's entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question again and got a yes. Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairytale complete with butterflies? The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

**(CNN) —** To hear the British media tell it, the June 2008 nuptials of Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin in Portofino, Italy, was an affront to good taste. 

Tabloid columnists and broadsheet commentators alike sharpened their knives, descriptor-slinging terms like "tacky," "ostentatious," and "vulgar" across the front pages. The £5 million price tag, the 16th-century abbey venue, the champagne-soaked Riviera yachting—all of it was held up as evidence of a modern celebrity culture gone hopelessly off the rails.

But behind the hand-wringing and elite sneering lies a much uglier reality: pure, unadulterated British class snobbery.

When royal princes or aristocratic heirs throw multi-million-pound weddings funded by taxpayers or inherited land wealth, the British press swoons. They praise the "tradition," the "glamour," and the "majesty" of it all. But when two 22-year-olds from one of Liverpool’s poorest council estates earn millions through raw, generational athletic talent and savvy personal branding, and decide to throw the party of a lifetime? Suddenly, it’s a crime against refinement.

It is time to call this criticism what it is: class warfare dressed up as cultural critique.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin represent a uniquely British success story, one that should be celebrated rather than mocked. They are not the product of elite public schools or dynastic wealth. They grew up in Croxteth, a tough, working-class district of Liverpool. They met at age 12, fell in love as teenagers, and stayed together as Wayne transformed from a prodigiously talented boy kicking a ball against brick walls into one of the greatest football players in the world. 

In the United States, we call this the American Dream—the idea that no matter where you start, sheer talent and grit can take you to the very top. In the eyes of the British establishment, however, the working class is apparently expected to "know its place." If they do manage to break through the ceiling, they are expected to act apologetic, hide their wealth, or adopt the understated sensibilities of the upper classes.

Wayne and Coleen refused to play that game. They earned their fortune, and they spent it making their dream wedding a reality, surrounded by the friends and family who knew them long before Wayne was making headlines at Old Trafford. 

What makes the British media’s vitriol even more hypocritical is what they routinely choose to ignore: the couple’s profound commitment to giving back. 

Much of the media’s fury was directed at the £2.5 million deal the couple struck with *OK! Magazine* for exclusive photo rights. Commentators sneered that it was a display of greed. Yet, what was quietly buried under the headlines was the fact that Wayne and Coleen requested guests not buy them gifts, asking instead for donations to be made to Claire House Children’s Hospice, a facility providing care to terminally ill children in Merseyside. The proceeds from their magazine deal were channeled directly into philanthropic endeavors, including the creation of the Wayne Rooney Foundation. 

While the pundits were busy critiquing Coleen’s dress and the lavishness of the venue, the couple was quietly raising millions for vulnerable children. 

The narrative that Wayne is just a "dumb footballer" and Coleen a "frivolous shopper" is a tired, paternalistic trope. Coleen built her own successful television and publishing career, proving herself to be a formidable businesswoman. Wayne carried the hopes of a football-obsessed nation on his shoulders from the age of 18, earning every penny through relentless physical sacrifice and world-class skill.

Why shouldn't two childhood sweethearts from Croxteth, who conquered the world on their own terms, celebrate their love in a sun-drenched Italian palace? 

The outrage over the Rooney wedding was never truly about the money. It was about who was spending it. It was about the discomfort of watching two working-class kids drink the finest champagne in a room built for dukes.

Wayne and Coleen Rooney didn't ruin Portofino; they crashed a party that the upper classes thought only belonged to them. And for that, they deserve a toast, not a lecture.

**THE OPINION COLUMN**

# Silk, Sin, and Snobbery: How Fleet Street’s Class War Was Fought at the Altar

**By Julian Vance**

In the summer of 2008, two high-profile British weddings caught the insatiable eye of the national press. Both took place under the soft glow of European sunshine, both involved vast sums of money, and both saw the private joy of young love traded to glossy celebrity magazines for eye-watering six-figure sums. 

Yet, to read the coverage at the time, you would be forgiven for thinking one was a sublime celebration of British heritage, and the other an apocalyptic assault on civilization itself.

The crime scene of the latter was Portofino, Italy. The culprits were Wayne Rooney, the generational footballing talent from Croxteth, Liverpool, and his teenage sweetheart, Coleen McLoughlin. Their wedding was a spectacular, unapologetic £5 million ($10 million) extravaganza spread over four days, complete with a 17th-century villa, a yacht, a performance by Westlife, and a record-breaking £2.5 million ($5 million) rights deal with *OK!* magazine.

Fleet Street, predictably, lost its collective mind. 

The commentary wasn’t merely critical of the extravagance; it was dripping with a distinctly British brand of aristocratic contempt. The Rooneys were branded "nouveau riche," "vulgar," and "ostentatious." Broadsheets and tabloids alike lined up to scoff at Coleen’s Marchesa dress, Wayne’s diamond-encrusted tastes, and the sheer, unadulterated "tackiness" of it all. The media commentary read less like entertainment reporting and more like an eviction notice served by the cultural elite. How dare two working-class kids from Scouse council estates spend *their own* hard-earned money with such unapologetic flair? 

Now, let us turn back the clock just a few weeks prior to May 2008, when Peter Phillips—the eldest grandson of Queen Elizabeth II—married Canadian Autumn Kelly at St George’s Chapel in Windsor Castle.

Mr. Phillips, a man whose primary achievement was being born into the right birth canal, engaged in the exact same commercial enterprise. He sold the exclusive photo rights of his wedding to *Hello!* magazine for a reported £500,000. He transformed the royal domain—and by extension, the British public's constitutional aesthetic—into a commercial backdrop for a celebrity rag. Members of the Royal Family were photographed for a paid feature like soap opera stars.

Was Phillips branded a tasteless mercenary? Was he subjected to psychological profiles probing the unrefined nature of his upbringing? 

Of course not. 

The press reaction to Phillips was overwhelmingly soft-focused, respectful, and forgiving. Where the Rooneys were called "cash-grabbing," Phillips was framed as "enterprising" or, at worst, guilty of a minor, modern misstep. His wedding was described as a "picturesque fairytale," a celebration of "enduring tradition." The commercialism was sanitized because the actors possessed the correct accents, the right lineage, and knew which fork to use for the fish course.

This stark double standard exposes the rotting core of classism in the British media. 

In the eyes of Fleet Street’s editorial boards—historically populated by the privately educated upper-middle classes—wealth is only acceptable if it is inherited, quiet, or draped in the velvet cloak of "tradition." When a royal monetizes their status, it is an eccentric modern update to the monarchy. When a footballer from a working-class background does it, it is a vulgar display of unearned vanity.

What the media hated about Wayne and Coleen was not the £5 million price tag. What they hated was their refusal to perform modesty. 

Wayne Rooney acquired his wealth through unprecedented physical genius and relentless work ethic, rising from the concrete pitches of Liverpool to the summit of global sport. Coleen built a media and fashion empire out of the intense scrutiny thrust upon her. They earned every penny. Yet, the British press mechanism exists to enforce a social curfew: *You may have the money, but you must never pretend you belong.*

The word "tacky" has long been weaponized by the upper classes as a linguistic cudgel to keep the parvenu in their place. It is a classist dog-whistle designed to signal that no matter how many millions a working-class person accumulates, they lack the "taste"—a code word for aristocratic indoctrination—to be truly legitimate. 

When Peter Phillips monetized Windsor Castle, he was framed as a noble negotiating the modern world. When Wayne and Coleen bought out a Italian villa, they were treated like lottery winners who didn't know how to act in a five-star restaurant.

Looking back, the Rooneys' Portofino spectacle was not a victory for vulgarity; it was a middle finger to the British class system. They took the millions offered by a media industry that exploited them daily, spent it on a glorious party for their working-class families in the Italian sun, and didn't apologize to a single columnist. 

The real vulgarity of 2008 was never the champagne in Portofino. It was the sneering snobbery of a media establishment that couldn't bear to see working-class kids enjoy the high life on their own terms.

Yet, for all the breathtaking excess, the most telling aspect of the wedding was its commercialization. The couple signed an exclusive deal with Britain’s *OK! Magazine*, selling the photo rights for an estimated $5 million. 

To traditionalists, selling your wedding photos to a glossy magazine was the height of tacky commercialism. But viewed through a modern lens, the Rooneys were early pioneers of a business model that now dominates the digital age. Long before the Kardashians built an empire by broadcasting their personal lives, and well before Instagram influencers began monetizing their engagements, Wayne and Coleen understood a fundamental truth of 21st-century fame: if the public is going to consume your personal life anyway, you might as well control the narrative—and take a cut of the profits.

There was also a poignant clash of class dynamics at play. The British press, historically uncomfortable with working-class people acquiring sudden, unbridled wealth, treated the wedding with a mixture of voyeuristic fascination and condescending judgment. Critics scoffed at the guest list, the security measures, and the sheer extravagance. 

Yet, for millions of young people from working-class backgrounds, Wayne and Coleen represented something else entirely: a rejection of traditional British reserve. They were kids from Croxteth who had conquered the world and were unashamed to spend their money exactly how they wanted to. It was loud, it was ostentatious, and to their fanbase, it was unapologetically real.

Sixteen years later, the Rooney marriage has endured trials that would have dissolved most high-profile unions. Through public scandals, intense tabloid intrusion, and the inevitable fading of Wayne’s playing career, they have remained together. Coleen has even reinvented herself as a master of public narrative—most famously through her meticulously executed "Wagatha Christie" legal saga, proving she was never just a passive participant in the celebrity machine.

When we look back at those photographs of Portofino in 2008—the blinding Italian sun, the oversized sunglasses, the $5 million magazine cover—it’s easy to dismiss it as the peak of 2000s consumerist absurdity. 

In truth, it was a turning point. Wayne and Coleen’s wedding was the moment celebrity culture shed its last illusions of privacy, trading intimacy for spectacle, and laying the groundwork for the modern, content-driven world we live in today. It was loud, expensive, and utterly fascinating—just like the era that created it.

counterfactuals.output:
**The Price of Royalty: Class War, Media Hypocrisy, and the Rooney Wedding**

In June 2008, the British media set its sights on Portofino, Italy, for what was framed as the ultimate spectacle of nouveau-riche excess: the £5 million wedding of England football star Wayne Rooney and his childhood sweetheart, Coleen McLoughlin. The four-day extravaganza featured a 17th-century villa, a luxury yacht, a performance by Westlife, and, most famously, a whimsical release of hundreds of live white butterflies into the Mediterranean breeze. 

To the tabloid press, however, these butterflies were not a symbol of romance; they were evidence of crimes against taste. 

The media coverage of the Rooney-McLoughlin nuptials remains a masterclass in journalistic hypocrisy—a stark illumination of how the British press fetishizes celebrity wealth while simultaneously weaponizing it to enforce class boundaries. 

For months surrounding the event, the commentary was drenched in snobbery. Tabloids and broadsheets alike engaged in a coordinated campaign of condescension, branding the couple with derogatory monikers like "Chav Royalty" and "Wayleen." The word *chav*—a viciously classist shorthand used to mock the working class—was deployed endlessly. The media scoffed at their extravagance, portraying the event as tacky, loud, and uncultured. 

Yet, this moral panic over "vulgar spending" ignored a fundamental truth: the press had created the very appetite for excess they were now condemning. The tabloids fed off the public’s obsession with celebrity lifestyles, building entire business models on paparazzi photos of Coleen’s shopping trips, only to turn around and print scolding editorials about her consumerism. 

What the media’s caricature conveniently erased was the genuine humanity and grounding at the heart of the couple's relationship. Long before the private jets and Italian villas, Wayne and Coleen were just two working-class kids growing up in Croxteth, Liverpool. Their love story didn't begin in a VIP lounge; it began on a suburban street corner when a 12-year-old Wayne stopped to help a young Coleen fix a slipped chain on her bicycle. This was not a romance manufactured by publicists, but a genuine bond forged in the gritty reality of northern, working-class Britain. But a grounded, enduring romance did not fit the media’s preferred narrative of mindless, fast-money hedonism.

Equally ignored was the nuance of Coleen’s own trajectory. The press routinely reduced her to the ultimate "WAG"—a passive, dependent consumer living off her partner's talent. In reality, Coleen was quietly building a formidable career of her own. By 2008, she was a successful columnist, TV presenter, author, and the face of major brand campaigns, earning millions independently. She had become a savvy business woman, yet the media insistently framed her success as mere luck, refusing to accord a working-class woman the professional respect routinely granted to middle-class style influencers today.

Perhaps the most glaring act of media hypocrisy, however, lay in the selective coverage of the wedding’s financial details. While headline-writers screamed about the £5 million price tag and the grandiosity of the butterfly release, they routinely buried the couple’s philanthropy in the fine print. 

Wayne and Coleen famously turned down traditional wedding gifts. Instead, they requested that their high-profile guests—and the media outlets bidding for coverage—donate to charity. Their wedding raised hundreds of thousands of pounds for Alder Hey Children’s Hospital in Liverpool and Clare House Children’s Hospice on the Wirral. These were not performative PR gestures, but deeply personal commitments to institutions supporting vulnerable children in their home region. 

Why did the press downplay this generosity? Because a couple using their moment of peak global attention to funnel money into children's hospitals completely undermined the narrative. It is impossible to sell the idea of "tacky, selfish, working-class lottery winners" when those same people are quietly funding life-saving medical equipment for local kids.

The media’s treatment of the 2008 Rooney wedding exposed a double standard that still exists today. When traditional blue-bloods or hereditary millionaires engage in displays of extravagant wealth, the press paints it as "tradition," "heritage," or "gala elegance." But when working-class individuals achieve success through extraordinary talent and enterprise, their spending is viewed as an intrusion into a world where they do not belong.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin were never forgiven by the cultural gatekeepers for daring to enjoy the fruits of their success on their own terms. The release of those butterflies in Portofino was meant to be a celebration of two young people who had beaten the odds together. The media, however, tried to turn it into a cautionary tale about wealth without breeding. In doing so, the press revealed far more about its own deep-seated class prejudices than it ever did about the couple at the altar.

LONDON, England (CNN) -- As the flashbulbs fade on the Italian Riviera following the £5 million wedding of Manchester United star Wayne Rooney and his childhood sweetheart, Coleen McLoughlin, the predictable chorus of cultural snobbery has reached a fever pitch. 

In the eyes of high-minded commentators and tabloid moralists, the four-day extravaganza in Portofino was a parade of modern vulgarity—a "tacky," over-the-top display of newly acquired wealth that epitomized everything wrong with contemporary celebrity culture. Critics point to the private jets, the glossy magazine deals, and the sheer scale of the expenditure as evidence of an obscene lack of restraint.

However, to reduce the union of Wayne and Coleen to a mere display of ostentatious wealth is to completely misunderstand their story. Far from being a lesson in bad taste, their fairytale wedding represents a profound triumph over adversity, class prejudice, and the brutal crucible of modern British fame.

To appreciate what this wedding truly signifies, one must look back at where it all began. Wayne and Coleen are not scions of inherited privilege. They grew up in Croxteth, a tough, working-class district of Liverpool where the odds are historically stacked against young people. When they met as young teenagers, there were no private jets or designer gowns—just a shared life in a community that knew struggle far better than luxury.

When Wayne was thrust into the international spotlight at the tender age of 16, carrying the impossible expectations of an entire football-obsessed nation on his shoulders, the pressure could have easily destroyed him. History is littered with the tragic stories of young athletes who succumbed to the overwhelming vices of sudden fame. Yet, through it all, Coleen remained his anchor, grounded in the same working-class values that shaped them both.

Coleen, too, faced her own immense adversity. Subjected to relentless, often cruel scrutiny by a media apparatus eager to mock her fashion sense, her physique, and her background, she was unfairly cast as the quintessential "WAG"—a lazy caricature designed to incite public envy and condescension. What the critics routinely ignored was her quiet resilience, her loyalty, and the dignity with which she navigated immense personal tragedy within her family, including her young sister’s lifelong fight against a debilitating illness. 

Instead of wilting under the spotlight, Coleen built her own career, transformed herself into a formidable businesswoman, and maintained an unwavering loyalty to the boy she fell in love with on the streets of Liverpool.

The outrage over the lavishness of their wedding reeks of a uniquely British strain of classism. When the aristocracy spends millions on historic castles and grand galas, it is celebrated as "patrimony" and "tradition." But when two working-class kids from Merseyside earn millions through world-class talent and sheer perseverance, and choose to spend that money celebrating their love with their family and friends, it is suddenly branded "chavvy" or "tacky."

Why should Wayne and Coleen apologize for their success? Wayne Rooney earned his fortune with his feet, through extraordinary skill, discipline, and hard work. Neither he nor Coleen stole a single penny of their wealth; they built it in the unrelenting arena of public life.

Their wedding was not a sign of bad taste—it was a joyous, unapologetic victory lap. It was a statement that two kids from Croxteth could survive the meat grinder of global celebrity, stay together through a decade of intense public pressure, and stand at the altar as equals on top of the world. 

Rather than sneering at the price tag, we should be celebrating a rare story of enduring loyalty and triumph against the odds. Wayne and Coleen's wedding wasn't tacky; it was the ultimate working-class fairytale.

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.
